Abstract

International shipping decarbonization has expanded beyond technical and operational regulation to include contested market-based bargaining. The proposed International Maritime Organization (IMO) Net-Zero Framework (NZF) combines a marine fuel standard with an economic compliance mechanism. Drawing on IMO submissions, voting records, official statements, and domestic and sectoral materials, this two-level game analysis examines why support sufficient to approve the draft for circulation in April 2025 did not translate into timely adoption later that year. The evidence suggests that the initial agreement space was not durable enough to support adoption on the planned timetable. At Level I, bargaining involved three linked dimensions: rule-making authority, responsibility allocation, and transition pathway design. At Level II, domestic, regional, and sectoral constraints included regulatory credibility and investment signals for the European Union; sovereignty and cost concerns for the United States; trade exposure and disproportionate impacts for trade-exposed emerging economies; ambition and revenue-supported transition for small island developing States; and fuel availability, fleet competitiveness, and legal certainty for energy exporters and open registries. A coalition sufficient at one procedural stage may therefore not remain sufficient at the next. A more durable agreement space would likely require an IMO-centered regulatory core, targeted enabling support, an ambition floor with compliance flexibility, and sequenced implementation and review.

1. Introduction

International shipping accounts for approximately 2% of global anthropogenic CO2 emissions, and its emissions trend remains closely linked to the growth of global trade [1] (p. 112). Effective and timely regulation of the sector’s greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions is therefore important to broader climate mitigation efforts [2]. Yet international shipping is not easily governed through conventional territorial approaches to emissions control. A ship may be owned, operated, financed, flagged, and fueled in different jurisdictions. The sector’s emissions are consequently addressed through a complex governance architecture involving the International Maritime Organization (IMO), Member States, regional organizations, industry associations, fuel suppliers, ports, shipowners, non-governmental organizations, and other public and private actors [3] (pp. 1–2). This cross-jurisdictional and multi-actor structure makes shipping decarbonization not only a technical and regulatory challenge, but also a political problem of coordinating divergent national and sectoral interests.

The 2023 IMO Strategy on Reduction of GHG Emissions from Ships marked an important step in this transition. It set the ambition of reaching net-zero GHG emissions from international shipping by or around 2050 and called for a basket of mid-term measures combining technical and economic elements [4] (paras. 3.3, 4.1, 4.5). The IMO Net-Zero Framework (NZF) represents the most developed attempt so far to translate these strategic commitments into proposed mandatory global rules. Set out as a proposed new Chapter 5 of Annex VI to the International Convention for the Prevention of Pollution from Ships (MARPOL), the IMO NZF comprises two linked regulatory pillars: a goal-based global marine fuel standard, expressed through GHG fuel intensity (GFI) requirements, and an economic compliance mechanism that assigns a price to GFI deficits, supports the uptake of zero- or near-zero-emission (ZNZ) technologies, fuels, and energy sources, and channels revenues through the IMO Net-Zero Fund [5] (Regs. 30–44). At its eighty-third session (MEPC 83) in April 2025, the IMO’s Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC) approved the draft amendments for circulation in advance of a separate adoption stage, with 63 votes in favor, 16 against, and 24 abstentions [6] (Annex 10).

The move from approval toward adoption nevertheless exposed the fragility of the emerging agreement space, understood here as the range of outcomes capable of supporting the coalition required at a particular procedural stage. The United States (U.S.) first announced that it would seek support from other IMO Member States to defeat the IMO NZF and later identified possible measures against supporting states, including restrictions on port access, visa and commercial penalties, additional port fees, and possible sanctions against officials [7,8]. In October 2025, the second extraordinary session of MEPC (MEPC/ES.2), convened to consider the adoption of the draft amendments, was adjourned for one year. The adjournment motion received 57 votes in favor, 49 against, and 21 abstentions [9]. Although the adjournment did not terminate the negotiations, the sequence suggests an unstable agreement space for market-based shipping decarbonization: the coalition sufficient to approve circulation of the draft text was not yet sufficiently broad and stable to secure adoption on the planned timetable. The reasons cannot be inferred from the outcome alone: unresolved technical, legal, and distributional questions remained relevant alongside external pressure and heterogeneous domestic, regional, and sectoral constraints.

Existing scholarship explains important components of this development along three main lines. One strand examines the technical and economic design of shipping decarbonization, including market-based measures (MBMs), alternative fuels, energy-efficiency gaps, and the value of combining policy mixes [10,11,12]. A second strand considers the legal foundations and distributive implications of IMO action, including the IMO’s regulatory mandate, the legal form of MARPOL Annex VI amendments, and the tension between uniform ship-based obligations and demands for differentiated or equitable treatment [13,14]. A third strand examines the governance of IMO policymaking, highlighting unequal participation, state–industry relationships, non-state actors, geopolitical conditions, and organizational practices [3,15,16]. Taken together, these studies explain many of the regulatory choices and legal-political disagreements surrounding shipping decarbonization. They do not, however, fully explain why support at the approval stage did not carry into timely adoption, or under what institutional conditions a more durable agreement space might be sustained.

The article addresses this question by applying the two-level game framework. In Robert D. Putnam’s formulation, governments bargain at Level I while remaining constrained by the range of outcomes acceptable at Level II, which constitutes an actor’s win-set [17] (pp. 434, 436–440). Drawing on this logic, the article uses agreement space to denote the range of outcomes acceptable to a coalition large enough to secure the required outcome at a given stage of the IMO process. An agreement space is durable when the necessary coalition can be maintained and the negotiated package remains acceptable under relevant Level II constraints as the process moves from approval to adoption, acceptance, entry into force, and implementation. Methodologically, the study combines process-oriented documentary analysis with a structured comparison of selected actors and actor groupings, while distinguishing documented Level I positions from evidence-based inferences concerning Level II constraints. Section 2.2 explains the framework’s adaptation to staged multilateral bargaining, while Section 2.3 specifies the observation period, documentary basis, and evidentiary approach.

This article makes three contributions. First, it offers a stage-ordered account of how the shift from energy-efficiency regulation to a package combining fuel standards, economic compliance, and revenue governance heightened political contestation, and why support sufficient for circulation at MEPC 83 was not sustained for timely adoption. Second, it shows that the IMO NZF negotiations cannot be reduced to a simple North–South or ambition-resistance divide; positions reflect cross-cutting constraints concerning rule-making authority, responsibility allocation, and transition pathway design. Third, it distinguishes stage-specific win-set overlap from a durable agreement space, focusing attention on how coalition requirements and the political costs of support may change across approval, adoption, acceptance, entry into force, and implementation. On this basis, it identifies four design conditions under which an environmentally meaningful package may also become politically supportable: an IMO-centered regulatory core, targeted enabling support, an ambition floor combined with compliance flexibility, and adaptive sequencing. In this sense, the IMO NZF also serves as an entry point into the broader politics of constructing politically sustainable regimes for international shipping decarbonization and global climate action [18] (p. 1).

The remainder of the article proceeds as follows. Section 2 traces the evolution from IMO energy-efficiency governance to market-based bargaining, sets out the analytical framework, and explains the evidentiary approach. Section 3 examines the Level I bargaining structure through three core questions: who should make the rules, how responsibility should be allocated, and how the transition pathway should be designed and paced. Section 4 examines the Level II constraints shaping selected negotiating actors and actor groupings. Section 5 assesses why approval-stage support did not translate into a coalition sufficient for timely adoption and considers alternative explanations for the adjournment. Section 6 examines the institutional conditions for a more durable agreement space, focusing on an IMO-centered regulatory core, targeted enabling support, flexible compliance pathways, and adaptive sequencing. Section 7 concludes.

2. International Shipping Decarbonization as a Two-Level Game

The sequence from approval for circulation to adjournment described above should be situated within a longer transformation in IMO climate governance. IMO regulation of shipping GHG emissions initially developed primarily through technical and operational efficiency measures. The turn toward MBMs, however, made questions of industrial adjustment, trade exposure, fuel transition, and the distribution of costs and revenues increasingly salient. This transformation provides the basis for examining the IMO NZF as a two-level game in which international bargaining interacts with domestic, regional, and sectoral constraints.

2.1. From Energy-Efficiency Governance to Market-Based Bargaining

The IMO’s work on shipping GHG emissions initially advanced through technical and operational measures. In 2003, the IMO Assembly directed the MEPC to evaluate technical, operational, and market-based options for limiting or reducing GHG emissions from international shipping [19] (para. 1(d)); in 2006, the MEPC formally incorporated all three categories into its regulatory agenda through an adopted work plan [20] (Annex 9, para. 3). These regulatory tracks progressed unevenly. The adoption of the Energy Efficiency Design Index (EEDI) and the Ship Energy Efficiency Management Plan (SEEMP) at MEPC 62 in 2011 introduced mandatory design-efficiency requirements for new ships and management-planning obligations for ships [21]. The IMO Data Collection System for fuel oil consumption, adopted in 2016, strengthened the information basis of the regime [22]. In 2021, the Energy Efficiency Existing Ship Index (EEXI) and the Carbon Intensity Indicator (CII) extended energy-efficiency regulation to existing ships and operational carbon intensity [23]. Together, these instruments embedded shipping decarbonization in ship-based standards, flag state administration, port state control, and established MARPOL compliance procedures.

This regulatory approach improved the efficiency of individual ships but could not by itself ensure absolute emissions reductions under continued growth in maritime transport. Long ship lifetimes and infrastructure lock-in also make delayed action especially risky [24]. MEPC 59 accordingly recognized in 2009 that technical and operational measures alone would be insufficient, and that MBMs could both strengthen investment incentives and generate resources for states requiring additional capacity and finance [25] (paras. 4.92–4.93 and 4.106). MBMs nevertheless carried more visible distributive consequences than ship-efficiency rules because they implicated carbon costs, revenue use, and the treatment of differently situated states and industries.

Those consequences contributed to a discontinuous negotiating process. Between 2010 and 2013, the IMO examined levy-based schemes, emissions trading schemes, efficiency credit trading arrangements, and hybrid mechanisms [26,27,28]. The proposals exposed disagreements over IMO competence, the relationship between uniform shipping rules and differentiated climate responsibilities, and the use of revenues. MEPC 65 suspended further discussion of MBMs and their impact assessments in 2013 [29] (para. 5.1). The regulatory groundwork for regional market-based governance then developed in the European Union (EU): the European Commission proposed a staged approach beginning with monitoring, reporting, and verification (MRV) and potentially culminating in a market-based measure [30] (p. 5), while Regulation (EU) 2015/757 applied from 2018 [31]. These developments did not resolve the IMO debate, but kept market-based governance on the policy agenda while intensifying concerns about regulatory fragmentation.

The multilateral agenda was revived through the 2018 Initial IMO Strategy on Reduction of GHG Emissions from Ships, which reintroduced market-based approaches by listing “new/innovative emission reduction mechanism(s), possibly including market-based measures, to incentivize GHG emission reduction” as a candidate mid-term measure for the period 2023 to 2030 [32] (para. 4.8.3). The 2023 IMO GHG Strategy went further by providing that the basket of candidate measures should comprise a goal-based marine fuel standard and an economic element based on maritime GHG emissions pricing [4] (para. 4.5). Member States, regional actors, and industry organizations subsequently advanced proposals on how these elements should be combined. In April 2025, MEPC 83 approved the draft MARPOL Annex VI amendments for circulation. The resulting NZF proposal links GFI requirements with economic compliance arrangements, reward incentives, and Net-Zero Fund governance. By combining a fuel standard with pricing and revenue use, it moved the IMO agenda beyond ship-efficiency regulation toward bargaining over the allocation of transition costs, support, and economic opportunities [33] (pp. 268–273). This shift made the acceptability of the emerging package more dependent on heterogeneous domestic, regional, and sectoral constraints.

2.2. Two-Level Bargaining in the IMO NZF Process

The distributive bargaining generated by the IMO NZF’s linked design makes the two-level game framework useful for examining how international negotiations interact with domestic, regional, and sectoral conditions. In Robert D. Putnam’s formulation, governments bargain at Level I while remaining constrained by the range of outcomes acceptable at Level II. This range constitutes an actor’s win-set, while overlap refers to the intersection of win-sets within which agreement is possible [17] (pp. 434, 436–440). A larger win-set may facilitate agreement but weaken bargaining leverage, whereas a narrower win-set may strengthen demands for concessions while increasing the risk of deadlock. Negotiators may also invoke or strategically present Level II constraints during international bargaining. Subsequent scholarship has further developed this reciprocal understanding of international and domestic politics by extending the framework to formal and informal forms of Level II acceptance and examining the roles of veto players, interest groups, delegated authority, and executive autonomy [34]. Its applications to trade, climate, and sectoral environmental negotiations provide useful points of comparison for the IMO NZF, as summarized in Table 1.

For the IMO NZF, the framework is applied in three related ways. First, an IMO outcome depends on a multilateral coalition capable of satisfying the decision rule applicable at a particular procedural stage. The relevant question is whether the proposed package falls within the win-sets of a coalition sufficient to support the required outcome at that stage. As the process moves from approval to adoption, acceptance, entry into force, and implementation, the composition of the relevant coalition and the political costs of continued support may change. Coalition sufficiency is therefore assessed separately at each stage. A coalition may remain viable while the package’s linked trade-offs are defensible at Level II and weaken when later stages expose costs, activate additional veto points, or unsettle earlier compromises. Second, Level II acceptance extends beyond formal treaty ratification. It concerns whether governments can politically defend, legally implement, and administratively sustain the emerging rules in light of domestic, regional, and sectoral constraints. These constraints may include existing legal commitments, political veto points, industry compliance capacity, fuel and port infrastructure, trade exposure, and administrative feasibility. In the case of EU Member States, national positions may also be shaped by regional legal and policy commitments. Third, Level I and Level II are mutually interactive rather than strictly sequential. Domestic, regional, and sectoral constraints operate throughout the negotiations, while draft rules, coalition signals, and external pressure may alter the political costs of support. This interaction is reinforced by the IMO NZF’s linked design, under which changes to one regulatory component may affect the acceptability of the package as a whole. Figure 1 summarizes the adapted two-level analytical framework used in this study.

2.3. Research Design and Evidentiary Approach

The analysis follows the IMO NZF negotiations across successive procedural stages and compares selected actors and actor configurations. The principal observation period runs from the adoption of the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy in July 2023 through 31 May 2026, encompassing MEPC 84 and the immediately subsequent amendment proposals. The corpus comprises attributable materials available through IMO documentation systems or public sources and relevant to the IMO NZF’s design, procedural status, or political acceptability. It includes IMO submissions and voting records, official national and regional statements, and where available, domestic policy and legislative documents, industry materials, and contextual economic and sectoral data.

The documents are organized through the framework in Table 2. The three Level I dimensions are drawn from the analytical framework, while some non-exclusive acceptance-condition codes—G, B, U, D, A, and F—were refined during the document review and are used as non-exclusive points of comparison. The unit of analysis is a documented observation bearing on an actor’s negotiating position, procedural stance, or relevant Level II constraint at a specified date and stage. Each observation records the actor, source, bargaining dimension, procedural stage, stated position, and available evidence of the underlying constraint. IMO submissions, votes, and diplomatic statements are used to identify Level I positions but are not treated as conclusive evidence of domestic causation. Inferences about Level II constraints are checked, where possible, against independent domestic, regional, sectoral, or economic materials. Procedural acts are interpreted only for the decision at issue. Table 2 sets out the resulting codes, observable indicators, and rules for stage-specific comparison and evidentiary assessment. For auditability, Supplementary Table S1 identifies the distinct documents included in the coded corpus, while Supplementary Table S2 maps the principal synthesized findings to the main underlying documents and observations.

The selected actor configurations are non-exclusive analytical groupings rather than exhaustive state classifications. They are identified by recurring combinations of observable legal, political, and economic exposure, including regional regulatory commitments, current domestic veto structures, trade exposure, climate and maritime vulnerability, hydrocarbon dependence, and fleet or registry exposure. The EU and U.S. are examined as distinctive institutional-political configurations, while the other three categories compare recurring patterns of constraint. Mixed cases may enter more than one grouping, and within-group variation is examined where actors’ positions or underlying exposures diverge. Because these indicators are not fully commensurable and the underlying public evidence remains uneven, the analysis reconstructs approximate boundaries of acceptability rather than assigning numerical scores or estimating win-set size. Non-state actors are not treated as separate win-set holders; their submissions and public positions are used to identify sectoral constraints, and where relevant, their influence on governmental bargaining positions.

3. Level I Bargaining: Three Dimensions of Contestation

At Level I, the IMO NZF raises three core bargaining issues: rule-making authority, responsibility allocation, and transition pathway design. Although examined separately, these dimensions are interdependent: institutional choices affect how obligations and support can be allocated, while distributive and transition concerns shape the acceptability of the resulting institutional package. Agreement on one dimension may therefore be undermined by unresolved disagreement on another, which helps explain why support for the package may change as it moves across procedural stages. Together, these dimensions organize the analysis below.

3.1. Rule-Making Authority: Who Should Make the Rules, and Through Which Forum?

The first dimension of contestation concerns rule-making authority. In legal and institutional terms, the IMO has long been treated as the central multilateral forum for regulating international shipping. Article 2(2) of the Kyoto Protocol to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (Kyoto Protocol) directed Annex I Parties to pursue the limitation or reduction in GHG emissions from marine bunker fuels through the IMO [42]. Article 1(a) of the Convention on the International Maritime Organization gives the IMO a broad mandate to encourage the general adoption of the highest practicable standards in matters concerning maritime safety, efficiency of navigation, and the prevention and control of pollution from ships [43]. Article 211(1) of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) requires state parties, acting through the competent international organization, to establish international rules and standards for the prevention, reduction, and control of vessel-source pollution [44]. The relevance of this framework to shipping GHG emissions is supported by the conclusion of the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (ITLOS) that anthropogenic GHG emissions constitute pollution of the marine environment under UNCLOS [45] (paras. 159–179). A compilation prepared by the United Nations Division for Ocean Affairs and the Law of the Sea (DOALOS) also identifies the IMO as the competent international organization for vessel-source pollution [46] (pp. 87–89). The case for IMO centrality is also functional: ship ownership, operation, flagging, fuel supply, and port use often span multiple jurisdictions, while uniform global standards can reduce regulatory fragmentation, competitive distortion, and regulatory avoidance. IMO-centered multilateralism has therefore generally served as the principal institutional pathway for international shipping decarbonization [47] (pp. 483–484).

The IMO’s central role in vessel-source regulation is widely recognized, but this does not imply agreement on the reach or content of its GHG rules. One line of disagreement concerns whether IMO rules are sufficiently ambitious and how they should interact with regional measures. When progress at the IMO is perceived as inadequate, pressure for action outside the organization may increase [13] (pp. 270–271). The EU’s extension of the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) to maritime transport and the adoption of FuelEU Maritime illustrate this dynamic [48,49]. These measures use calls at EU ports as an important basis for their application and are often presented as responses to insufficient global progress. Yet the application of EU rules to voyages linked to non-EU ports has raised concerns about extraterritorial effects and compliance burdens arising from overlapping rules [50,51]. Regional and global measures should therefore not be viewed as simple alternatives. Regional rules may produce divergent standards, but they may also increase pressure on the IMO to adopt more stringent global rules [52] (pp. 88–98). Similar dynamics may arise as national or regional measures develop elsewhere, although their legal form and maturity may differ.

A second issue concerns the institutional reach of MARPOL-based rule-making. MARPOL Annex VI has already been used to adopt technical and operational energy-efficiency measures. The IMO NZF would extend this framework by combining fuel-intensity requirements with an economic compliance mechanism, a registry, and an IMO-administered fund [5] (regs. 35–41). Supporters of this architecture have treated these functions as sector-specific mechanisms ancillary to compliance with the GFI standard and the reduction in vessel-source emissions. Several opposing states have instead argued that mandatory payments by shipping companies and the administration of the resulting revenues are not adequately grounded in MARPOL Annex VI and move the IMO toward a contested fiscal function [53] (paras. 3–5 and 16–23). The dispute therefore concerns both the legal basis of these functions and the political consensus and transparency required for their development within a member-state-led organization [54] (p. 4).

A third issue concerns legal form and amendment procedure. The IMO NZF was prepared as an amendment to MARPOL Annex VI. If adopted, it would be subject to the tacit acceptance procedure under Article 16(2)(f)(ii) and (iii) of MARPOL. Under this procedure, an amendment is deemed accepted unless the prescribed threshold of objections is reached within a prescribed period [55]. At MEPC 84, the U.S. argued instead, that given the significance and potential effects of a global shipping decarbonization agreement, proposals at MEPC should follow an explicit acceptance procedure. This procedure would require affirmative acceptance by parties before the resulting obligations become binding [56] (para. 6.5). In contrast, the EU’s formal position at MEPC 84 was to support the tacit acceptance procedure [57] (Annex, Orientations (2) and (3)(a)–(b)). The choice between tacit and explicit acceptance affects both the consent threshold and parties’ control over when the resulting obligations become binding. It may therefore affect whether an adoption-stage coalition translates into sufficiently broad participation.

3.2. Responsibility Allocation: Uniform Obligations and Differentiated Equity

The second dimension of Level I contestation concerns responsibility allocation. IMO shipping regulation has generally relied on non-discriminatory, ship-based obligations. Article 227 of UNCLOS prohibits formal or practical discrimination against vessels of other states in the application of marine-pollution rules [44]. Article 5(4) of MARPOL similarly requires parties to apply its requirements to ships of non-Parties as necessary to ensure that such ships receive no more favorable treatment [55]. This non-discriminatory regulatory approach can facilitate port state control, limit competitive distortion, and reduce regulatory avoidance [58] (p. 9). Climate governance, however, emphasizes differentiated equity [59]. Principle 7 of the Rio Declaration on Environment and Development, Article 3(1) of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, and Article 2(2) of the Paris Agreement express related, but not identical, formulations of equity and common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities (CBDR-RC) [60,61,62].

The IMO’s strategies have sought to accommodate both approaches. The 2018 Initial IMO Strategy on Reduction of GHG Emissions from Ships stated that both non-discrimination and no more favorable treatment, on the one hand, and CBDR-RC in light of different national circumstances, on the other hand, should be taken into account [32] (para. 3.2.1). The 2023 IMO Strategy on Reduction of GHG Emissions from Ships retained this balance, added a commitment to a just and equitable transition, and required the impacts of proposed measures on states to be assessed, with particular attention to developing countries, especially least developed countries (LDCs) and small island developing states (SIDS) [4] (paras. 2, 3.5.1, 3.5.3, 4.5, 4.10, and 5.3).

In the IMO NZF negotiations, these principles frame disagreements over core obligations, revenue use, and support [63] (pp. 1–3). Some actors favor generally uniform ship-based obligations to preserve enforcement and limit avoidance. Others give greater weight to equity and capacity constraints. Economic studies suggest that formally uniform carbon-pricing measures may still have uneven effects because additional shipping costs can raise freight rates and import prices, especially in trade-dependent economies [64,65]. Formally uniform obligations may also have uneven implementation effects because monitoring, enforcement, fuel infrastructure, and administrative capacity remain uneven across states. The practical question is therefore where differentiation should occur: in core obligations or compliance timelines, revenue allocation, financial and technological support, compliance flexibility, or a combination of these elements. One possible compromise is to retain generally uniform ship-based obligations while differentiating enabling support and allowing time-limited, reviewable flexibility for capability constraints. Whether this combination widens the agreement space depends on the design and safeguards of the differentiated elements.

3.3. Transition Pathway Design: Regulatory Ambition and Commercial Feasibility

The third dimension of Level I contestation concerns the direction and pace of the transition required by the regime. Within the IMO NZF package, the GFI targets determine how quickly ships must reduce the lifecycle emissions of their fuel mix. Ships performing beyond the direct compliance target may generate surplus units that can be banked or transferred, whereas ships exceeding the applicable GFI thresholds must balance their compliance deficit through surplus units or remedial units acquired by making contributions to the IMO Net-Zero Fund. Remedial-unit prices and the availability of surplus units shape whether operators switch fuels, acquire compliance units, or pay into the Fund, while rewards for ZNZ fuels influence investment in new fuels and technologies. Meanwhile, lifecycle rules determine which fuels receive regulatory credit. These components operate jointly: a stringent GFI trajectory combined with inexpensive remedial compliance may produce different investment and distributional effects from a more moderate trajectory paired with a stronger economic signal. In either case, lifecycle treatment and fuel availability shape the practical options and costs faced by operators.

Level I bargaining therefore concerns how ambition and feasibility should be calibrated. An ambition-led approach emphasizes a credible GFI trajectory and a price signal strong enough to induce investment before ZNZ fuels become widely available. A feasibility-led approach gives greater weight to fuel affordability, availability, scalability, and existing infrastructure, and therefore favors greater flexibility or slower adjustment. These different weightings are visible in the amendments circulated after the 2025 adjournment. For example, Tuvalu opposed any erosion of the existing level of ambition and proposed that subsequent amendments should only strengthen it [66] (Annex 1, p. 1). Liberia instead proposed linking the GFI trajectory to “Commercially Viable Fuels”, assessed by reference to affordability, availability, and scalability [67] (Annex, regs. 2.3.16–2.3.20). Comparable research in another hard-to-abate transport sector also indicates that the scalability of alternative-fuel pathways depends on technical practicability, economic feasibility, and supporting policy frameworks [68] (pp. 1, 10).

Lifecycle accounting creates a related contest over what qualifies as a low-emission fuel. Because the draft IMO Net-Zero Framework applies a well-to-wake approach, system boundaries, default emission factors, and certification rules affect the compliance value assigned to each fuel pathway [69] (paras. 1, 2.1–2.2, 8.1). These choices may favor some fuel and investment pathways over others. A joint submission by the International Chamber of Shipping and five other industry associations called for representative default emission factors, internationally recognized data standards, and regular review [70] (paras. 3, 5–9).

4. Level II Win-Sets: Constraints in Major Actor Configurations

This section turns from the Level I bargaining structure to the Level II constraints that shape the acceptability of the IMO NZF in domestic, regional, and sectoral settings. It examines five selected configurations: the EU, the U.S., trade-exposed emerging economies, SIDS, and energy exporters/open registries. Following Section 2.3, these configurations are non-exclusive and internally heterogeneous, and the resulting boundaries of acceptability remain indicative.

4.1. European Union (EU)

The EU is treated here as a regulatory-forerunner operating through a regional structure [71] (pp. 1256–1259). EU institutions and Member States coordinate positions for IMO negotiations, but regional commitments, national preferences, and sectoral interests need not be identical. This configuration is rooted in an established regional pathway. Regulation (EU) 2015/757 created an MRV system that generates publicly available data covering maritime emissions [31,72], which subsequently provided part of the information infrastructure for incorporating maritime transport into the EU ETS from 2024 [48] (art. 1.3). In parallel, FuelEU Maritime introduced progressively stricter limits on the GHG intensity of energy used on board ships [49]. Together with the European Climate Law, these measures have incorporated shipping into the EU’s wider climate-neutrality pathway [73].

This body of regional law constitutes a significant Level II constraint. Because shipping is already incorporated into EU climate law, the IMO NZF is assessed against an existing regulatory baseline rather than a blank slate. The EU’s position at the IMO is therefore conditioned by existing legal commitments, carbon-market credibility, and an interest in maintaining regional regulatory leadership [74] (p. 244), often described as the Brussels Effect [75]. Council Decision (EU) 2025/2093 formally established that EU Member States acting jointly in the interest of the Union should support the adoption of the new Chapter 5 of MARPOL Annex VI containing the IMO NZF [76] (arts. 1–3). European Shipowners similarly supported the framework as a means of strengthening regulatory certainty, creating incentives for cleaner fuels, and maintaining an international level playing field [77]. The formal EU mandate and the cited sectoral position therefore converge on support for a credible global framework. Otherwise, a weak global agreement would risk making EU regional measures appear either excessive or competitively harmful.

This context shapes the EU’s approach to rule-making authority. The EU generally supports IMO-centered multilateralism because a global framework can reduce regulatory fragmentation and create a broader market for transition investments. The adjournment of the adoption discussions at MEPC/ES.2 delayed the EU’s preferred multilateral approach and added to the regulatory uncertainty facing the European shipping sector [78] (pp. 17–18). Meanwhile, the EU ETS and FuelEU Maritime provide regional fallback options. The EU ETS review clause expressly links the future scope of the regional system to the outcome of the IMO process [48] (art. 1.7). The EU therefore prefers an IMO-centered framework, but its support depends partly on whether that framework remains compatible with its existing regional regulatory framework.

In terms of responsibility allocation, the EU’s position is consistent with generally uniform core obligations combined with targeted enabling support. Its regional measures apply according to ships and voyages rather than the development status of flag states [79] (pp. 360–365). At the IMO, an EU-sponsored submission proposed using revenues to support a just and equitable transition, SIDS and LDCs, research and development, and ZNZ incentives [80] (paras. 6–7). Earlier European Commission funding for the IMO’s Global Maritime Technology Cooperation Center Network provides a separate example of capacity-building support [81]. Together, these materials locate differentiation primarily in revenue use and enabling support rather than in core obligations imposed on ships.

On transition pathway design, the EU’s acceptable range is closely tied to regulatory credibility. Its negotiating position has supported the predictable tightening of GFI requirements, a meaningful economic signal, and incentives for ZNZ fuels [80] (paras. 6–7). After the adjournment, Council Decision (EU) 2026/1067 opposed removing the approved NZF while permitting consensus-building changes consistent with the 2023 Strategy and future adoption [57]. This indicates room for bounded adjustment, although the available evidence suggests less room for changes that remove the economic element, materially weaken the GFI trajectory, or erode the market signal. The EU’s position can therefore be interpreted as ambition-oriented but shaped by existing regional commitments. It supports IMO centrality, targeted assistance, and some implementation flexibility, provided that these elements do not undermine the regulatory and investment signals already embedded in EU law.

4.2. United States (U.S.)

The U.S. is best understood as a configuration shaped by the current administration’s domestic constraints. Under the second Trump administration, the relevant Level II constraints include consumer-cost politics, sovereignty concerns, anti-tax framing, energy interests, and maritime industrial policy. An August 2025 interagency statement described the IMO NZF as a “global carbon tax”, arguing that it would increase energy and transport costs and disadvantage U.S.-linked liquefied natural gas (LNG) and biofuel pathways [7]. The statement indicates that the proposed mandatory economic element, centralized revenue mechanism, and binding schedule of fuel-intensity reductions fall outside the administration’s current acceptable range.

This position is reinforced by wider industrial and geopolitical priorities. Executive Order 14269 linked the rebuilding of the U.S. maritime industrial base to national security and economic prosperity while emphasizing the asymmetry between the U.S. and China in commercial shipbuilding [82] (secs. 1–5). The United States Trade Representative’s Section 301 action on “China’s Targeting of the Maritime, Logistics, and Shipbuilding Sectors for Dominance” likewise treated dependence on Chinese ships and maritime components as an economic-security and supply-chain risk and introduced responsive service fees and tariff measures [83]. A June 2025 letter from the Vice Chairman of the House Ways and Means Committee, drawing on concerns expressed by a Florida shipping business, argued that the IMO NZF would increase costs and strengthen China’s shipbuilding position [84]. In the current political setting, the framework can therefore be portrayed not only as a climate obligation, but also alongside maritime-industrial recovery and strategic competition with China.

The wider U.S. policy and sectoral setting is not uniformly opposed to maritime decarbonization. The federal “Action Plan for Maritime Energy and Emissions Innovation”, issued under the previous administration in December 2024, pursued near-total reductions in maritime GHG emissions by 2050 and sought to scale low- and net-zero-emission fuels alongside shipbuilding capacity and port infrastructure [85] (p. 1). Sectoral preferences are also not uniform. The Chamber of Shipping of America supported a single global system rather than multiple regional regimes that could expose vessels to overlapping emissions charges [86]. These positions do not make the existing framework acceptable to the current administration, but the contrast with present executive policy cautions against treating the U.S. position as permanent or uniformly shared.

The current constraints are reflected across the three Level I dimensions. On rule-making authority and procedure, the U.S. post-adjournment submission argued that the IMO NZF would extend the IMO beyond its mission and opposed further consideration of the existing architecture [56] (paras. 2, 4, and 6.1–6.5). On responsibility allocation, the U.S. adoption-stage submission criticized the proposed fund as redistributive and opposed preferential treatment for particular fuels, technologies, or countries [87] (paras. 4 and 5.4). On transition pathway design, the post-adjournment submission rejected economic penalties, levies, and multilateral funds while favoring an “energy-all” approach that would not disadvantage conventional fuels, LNG, nuclear energy, biomass fuels, or other propulsion technologies. It also emphasized the reliability of existing fleets and targets based on current market conditions rather than predetermined end states [56] (paras. 6.1–6.3). Together, these materials indicate that the present administration’s acceptable range largely excludes a package combining mandatory economic contributions, a centralized fund, and a predetermined schedule of fuel-intensity reductions perceived to penalize incumbent fuels. The evidence suggests that this position is reinforced by some congressional, energy, and maritime-industrial concerns, but it does not establish a unified or permanent domestic consensus.

4.3. Differentiated Global South and Related Actor Configurations

Many actors conventionally placed within the Global South share concerns about equity, implementation capacity, technology access, development priorities, and disproportionately negative impacts. These concerns do not, however, generate a single Level II acceptance boundary. Trade-exposed emerging economies, SIDS, and energy exporters/open registries approach the IMO NZF under different economic and institutional positions. The following groupings compare recurring conditions rather than fixed negotiating blocs. Their internal variation helps explain why the IMO NZF could attract substantial Global-South support at MEPC 83 while remaining contested at the formal adoption stage.

4.3.1. Trade-Exposed Emerging Economies

Trade-exposed emerging economies represent a conditional-support configuration. Their commonality lies in exposure to the distributive effects of shipping decarbonization. Their recurring Level II constraints include trade-related cost increases, pressures on export competitiveness and essential imports, development priorities, and uneven access to transition finance, fuels, technology, and infrastructure [88]. These constraints can favor an IMO-centered global framework over fragmented regional regulation, which could multiply compliance costs and create competitive asymmetries. China, India, and Brazil all supported the approval of the draft amendments for circulation at MEPC 83 [6] (Annex 10). Their positions nevertheless diverged at MEPC/ES.2: Brazil opposed the motion to adjourn, whereas China and India supported it [9]. Brazil subsequently proposed retaining the principal architecture of the IMO NZF while moderating its pre-2035 schedule of GFI reductions and adjusting its compliance and fund arrangements [89] (Annex 2, regs. 35–41). These materials indicate continued engagement in IMO rule-making, but not common acceptance of the framework’s ambition, timing, financing, or distributional effects.

In responsibility allocation and transition pathway design, the principal overlap lies in combining generally uniform ship-based obligations with differentiated implementation and access to transition support. Domestic evidence nevertheless indicates different cost–opportunity balances. In Brazil, a public call worth 6 billion Brazilian reais (BRL) received 33 proposals concerning maritime fuels, while commercial and pilot uses of marine biofuel blends indicate an emerging domestic fuel base [90] (Section 9.5, pp. 66–68). This makes the lifecycle treatment and eligibility of biofuel pathways particularly relevant. India has linked its support for the IMO NZF to differentiated responsibilities [91] (paras. 2–6) while allocating 1.15 billion Indian rupees (INR) to green-hydrogen shipping pilots involving ship retrofits and port bunkering facilities [92]. This reflects both industrial interest and continuing dependence on phased infrastructure development and public support. China has emphasized CBDR-RC and different national circumstances [93]. Its green-shipbuilding policies seek a leading global position by 2030 [94], and Chinese shipyards obtained more than 70% of global green-vessel orders during the first three quarters of 2024 [95]. A 2026 Maritime Safety Administration opinion also sets objectives concerning shipping standards, emissions monitoring, bunkering capacity, professional skills, and participation in international rule-making [96]. These sectoral conditions do not by themselves determine negotiating positions, but they affect the balance between trade-related costs and transition opportunities.

Across these cases, the agreement space is likely broader where an IMO-centered framework limits regulatory fragmentation, provides safeguards against disproportionate cost pass-through, recognizes multiple credible transition pathways, and makes finance, technology, and incentives accessible to developing economies. It is likely narrower where the economic element globalizes costs without providing comparable access to transition benefits. Within this broad pattern, Brazil places greater emphasis on GFI reductions and the recognition of biofuels; India on differentiated implementation and capacity support; and China on distributional treatment and the industrial effects of technical standards.

4.3.2. Small Island Developing States (SIDS)

SIDS are treated here as an ambition-and-support configuration. Their shared Level II constraints arise from acute climate vulnerability, dependence on maritime connectivity for food, fuel, and other essential imports, limited fiscal capacity, and uneven access to transition finance [97,98,99]. The climate policies of the Marshall Islands and Fiji provide additional evidence of the domestic salience of vulnerability, resilience, and implementation capacity [100,101]. These conditions create a dual constraint: delayed or inadequate decarbonization aggravates long-term climate risks, while measures that raise transport costs without adequate support may intensify immediate affordability and food-security pressures. This combination helps explain why SIDS have acted as policy entrepreneurs for ambitious but distributionally responsive shipping regulation [102] (pp. 831–838). Some SIDS also maintain major open registries: in 2025, the Marshall Islands accounted for 12.5% of global fleet capacity in deadweight tons, making registry competitiveness an additional consideration [103].

For SIDS, rule-making authority is closely connected to effectiveness. An IMO-centered regime offers broad emissions coverage and a common institutional basis for collecting and allocating revenues, but its value depends on timely and sufficiently ambitious action. The joint proposal by the Marshall Islands and Solomon Islands combined a universal levy with a sequenced fuel standard as an equitable package [104] (paras. 6–17 and 23–31), while a later SIDS-led proposal sought to keep the IMO NZF aligned with commitments already made by IMO and its Member States [105]. A joint submission by ten SIDS and the International Chamber of Shipping further proposed that revenues support alternative-fuel and port infrastructure, seafarer training, capacity-building, mitigation of disproportionately negative impacts, and adaptation and resilience in climate-vulnerable states [99] (paras. 14–29). Taken together, these positions support not carbon pricing in isolation, but a credible emissions signal coupled with accessible transition support.

Procedural conduct also requires careful interpretation. At MEPC 83, a group of ten SIDS formally criticized the approved draft for insufficient climate ambition and inadequate revenue generation [6] (para. 7.44); most of the same delegations later voted against adjournment at MEPC/ES.2 [9]. These acts show that dissatisfaction with the package could coexist with opposition to delaying its consideration. The opposition of SIDS to substantially weakening a framework they already regarded as falling short of 1.5 °C alignment marks the ambition boundary [106] (paras. 4–10, 15, and 19–21); the revenue proposal marks the distributional boundary [99] (paras. 3 and 13–30). A weak or delayed framework would fail to address their climate constraints, whereas economic obligations without credible support could exceed their cost and capacity constraints. SIDS can therefore align with the EU on an ambition floor and with trade-exposed emerging economies on revenue access and impact mitigation.

4.3.3. Energy Exporters and Open Registries

Energy exporters and open registries are treated here as differentiated asset-protection configurations. The grouping does not presume identical economic structures or preferences, but captures a shared concern with how the transition affects incumbent fuel and fleet assets. Energy exporters are principally exposed through hydrocarbon revenues, bunkering markets, and fuel-production infrastructure. Open registries are more directly concerned with fleet competitiveness, registry income, and the compliance burdens imposed on globally mobile ships. These interests are economically significant: Liberia, Panama, and the Marshall Islands together accounted for 45.1% of world fleet capacity in deadweight tons in 2025 [103] (pp. 50–51). The Marshall Islands’ support for a universal levy also demonstrates that registry exposure does not determine a single substantive preference [104] (paras. 1 and 31). The grouping therefore identifies recurring concerns about commercial feasibility and fuel availability, rather than a coherent negotiating bloc.

These different exposures shape their approach to rule-making authority and responsibility allocation. Both configurations may prefer IMO-centered regulation because a single global framework can reduce regional fragmentation and competitive distortion. For energy exporters, however, IMO centrality does not remove concerns about the legal and distributive reach of the framework. International Energy Agency (IEA) regional data indicate the continuing economic importance of hydrocarbons in the Middle East, although such regional evidence cannot establish identical national preferences [107]. Several states questioned whether MARPOL Annex VI could support mandatory payments by shipping companies to an IMO-administered fund [53] (paras. 3–5 and 16–23), while a broader submission emphasized the need to safeguard international trade, food and energy security, and economic development [108] (para. 5). Open registries place greater weight on uniform implementation and manageable compliance, but do not form a unified anti-pricing bloc. Liberia and Panama, for example, co-sponsored a proposal treating a levy or contribution as an indispensable economic element [109] (paras. 3 and 9). The evidence instead points to recurring but differently weighted concerns about legal authority, cost effects, administration, and the adjustment of existing fuel and fleet assets.

Commercial feasibility is especially important to transition pathway design. In 2026, Argentina, Liberia, and Panama proposed replacing the centralized Fund and adjusting scheduled GFI reductions according to the affordability, availability, and scalability of marine fuels [110] (paras. 5–15). The evidence therefore does not support a single acceptance boundary for energy exporters and open registries. Interest in global fuel standards may coexist with changing positions on pricing, revenue collection, and the pace of GFI reductions. Agreement is more likely where the legal basis is sufficiently clear, compliance costs remain predictable, and compliant fuels can be supplied at scale. It is less likely where regulation is perceived as imposing abrupt asset devaluation, commercially unavailable fuel requirements, or open-ended financial obligations. These concerns may also generate limited overlap with trade-exposed emerging economies on fuel affordability, competitiveness, and implementation flexibility, without erasing the differences in their underlying Level II constraints.

5. Diagnostic Synthesis: Sources of Instability in the Agreement Space

The preceding analysis helps explain why support sufficient to approve the draft for circulation did not produce a coalition capable of securing adoption on the planned timetable. Approval for circulation was a legally consequential step, but it showed only that a coalition sufficient for that procedural step was willing to keep the package under consideration. It did not establish that the same states regarded the draft as acceptable for adoption under their respective Level II conditions. Under Article 16 of MARPOL, adoption required a separate two-thirds majority of the parties present and voting [55]. The adjournment at MEPC/ES.2 therefore indicates that the stage-specific agreement space had not become sufficiently stable for adoption on the planned timetable. Continued work around MEPC 84 further shows that the negotiations remained open.

Four interacting mechanisms offer plausible explanations. First, several elements of the linked NZF package continued to attract disagreement or required further specification, including remedial-unit pricing, Fund governance and revenue allocation, the pace of GFI reductions, fuel eligibility and availability, and implementation arrangements. This may have enabled some delegations to support circulation while reserving their positions on the package to be considered for adoption. Second, objections concerning the legal basis of the economic compliance mechanism and the use of tacit rather than explicit acceptance introduced additional concerns about institutional authority and procedural consent. Third, as adoption became more immediate, the framework’s cost, distributional, and industrial consequences may have become more politically salient across different Level II settings. Fourth, the U.S. position shifted to an overtly oppositional Level I strategy under the present administration. It may have affected other actors through direct pressure, reduced confidence in the framework’s political viability, or political cover for pre-existing objections. These mechanisms are therefore treated as interacting sources of instability rather than independently demonstrated causes.

Taken together, the documentary record suggests that the approval-stage coalition was procedurally sufficient but substantively heterogeneous. Actors associated continued engagement with different combinations of IMO centrality, economic-governance safeguards, differentiated support, regulatory ambition, and implementation feasibility. These conditions could coexist at the circulation stage without amounting to shared acceptance of the complete package for adoption. Across the selected configurations, three possible bridge patterns recur. The first combines an IMO-centered framework with bounded and reviewable economic governance. The second combines generally uniform ship-based obligations with differentiated enabling support. The third combines a credible ambition floor with fuel and technology openness and feasible implementation. These patterns identify elements of a possible package around which a coalition sufficient for a later procedural stage might be assembled. Their ability to broaden the agreement space would depend on credible institutional safeguards, accessible support, and flexibility that does not undermine regulatory ambition. These elements cannot, by themselves, accommodate the present U.S. administration’s rejection of mandatory pricing and centralized Fund governance. Section 6 considers how they might contribute to a more durable agreement space.

6. Pursuing a More Durable Agreement Space: Policy Implications

The preceding analysis identifies recurring acceptance conditions that may help sustain the coalition required at later procedural stages. The implications below are therefore conditional design propositions. Four implications follow: preserving IMO centrality while bounding economic governance, targeting enabling support, combining an ambition floor with compliance flexibility, and using adaptive sequencing to maintain acceptability across successive stages.

6.1. Preserving IMO Centrality While Bounding Economic Governance

The first implication concerns rule-making authority. IMO centrality remains important because international shipping operates across jurisdictions and benefits from globally comparable rules. An IMO-centered framework may reduce regulatory fragmentation across trade routes and flag jurisdictions while extending comparable obligations beyond EU-linked voyages and supporting the EU’s interest in a credible global transition. It can therefore provide a shared institutional starting point even where actors disagree over the content of the rules.

IMO centrality does not, however, resolve disagreements over the scope of IMO authority. For actors concerned about sovereignty, fiscal authority, or institutional overreach, acceptability depends partly on whether pricing, revenue collection, and allocation functions remain within a clearly defined regulatory mandate. From a design perspective, bounded economic governance requires registry operation, revenue collection, and support functions to remain clearly connected to compliance with the GFI regime. Although comparative practice across multilateral funds does not identify a single required governance model, it supports making explicit the purposes and permitted uses of revenues, governing-body composition and procedures, eligibility and access rules, implementing arrangements, reporting and disclosure, independent audit, and periodic review [111] (paras. 5–23). Technical input from shipping companies, fuel suppliers, ports, and other non-state actors may inform implementation and review, but regulatory and allocation decisions should remain transparent and subject to Member State authority. Such safeguards are unlikely to overcome opposition to mandatory pricing or centralized revenue collection in principle. They may nevertheless make the framework more defensible for conditional supporters concerned with institutional overreach, centralized control over revenues, or mandate expansion.

IMO centrality also requires coordination with regional/national measures. Existing regional measures, including the EU ETS and FuelEU Maritime, form part of the legal and political setting in which an IMO agreement would operate. Meanwhile, overlapping regimes may create duplicate costs, inconsistent accounting, and regulatory spillovers. Further regional or national measures may increase the value of global coordination by raising the costs of fragmentation, but they may also provide fallback pathways that reduce the immediate urgency of compromise at the IMO or entrench divergent standards. A future IMO framework could therefore provide for a mechanism to review compatibility with regional and national measures, covering reporting requirements, lifecycle accounting, overlapping financial obligations, and environmental integrity. Such a mechanism should facilitate coordination without automatically treating different regimes as equivalent or allowing compatibility arrangements to weaken the global ambition floor.

6.2. Targeting Enabling Support and Revenue Use

The second implication concerns enabling support and the use of revenues generated by the framework. Revenue governance may help make a formally uniform Level I package more defensible across heterogeneous Level II settings. Ship-based obligations can support consistent enforcement and limit competitive distortion, but their effects may remain unequal when compliance costs are transmitted through freight rates and import prices, or when access to fuels, infrastructure, and finance differs across states [64,65]. Related supply-chain research suggests that the environmental and welfare effects of transportation-based carbon penalties depend on how the burden is allocated among market actors and on the design of accompanying support [112]. Accordingly, generally uniform core obligations may be combined with differentiation in eligibility for enabling support and in the allocation of revenues.

In this regard, targeted support is intended to address identifiable constraints that make uniform obligations more difficult to implement or defend at Level II. For the EU, such support can preserve the level-playing-field logic of ship-based obligations while strengthening the investment signal for ZNZ fuels. For the U.S., such support is unlikely by itself to overcome current objections to mandatory pricing and an IMO-administered fund. A narrowly defined, transparent, and reviewable arrangement may nevertheless reduce concerns about open-ended redistribution or unchecked fiscal expansion among actors whose objections concern institutional scope and oversight rather than the economic compliance mechanism in principle. For SIDS and trade-exposed emerging economies, as well as for some energy exporters and open registries, relevant needs may include different combinations of resilience, fuel access, infrastructure, certification, administrative capacity, and workforce adjustment. These needs vary within each grouping and should not create automatic entitlements. Table 4 links potential forms of support to the Level II constraints they are intended to address.

The precise institutional form through which these functions would be performed remains contested. Where revenues are administered through an IMO fund, the four windows could operate within a single architecture rather than through separate funds. The MEPC may define common eligibility, access, and allocation criteria, while a representative governing body applies those criteria and reports allocations and outcomes by window. Access modalities and implementing arrangements should also be specified, including whether support is accessed directly or through accredited or designated implementing partners [111] (paras. 18–19). Independent audit, periodic review, published allocation data, and safeguards against conflicts of interest and double counting would help limit administrative complexity, capture risks, and mandate expansion. Any alternative arrangement performing comparable support functions should meet comparable standards of access, transparency, audit, and review.

6.3. Combining an Ambition Floor with Feasible Compliance Pathways

The third implication concerns transition pathway design. A more durable agreement space would likely require both a credible ambition floor and flexible compliance pathways. The floor should comprise progressively tightening GFI requirements, a compliance signal capable of sustaining incentives for direct compliance and ZNZ investment, and review arrangements that preserve the framework’s overall direction. The pace of GFI reductions, the cost of remedial compliance, and ZNZ rewards should be considered together: if requirements tighten faster than eligible fuels and supporting infrastructure can expand, compliance costs may rise without equivalent near-term fuel switching [12] (p. 7). An overly weak signal may reduce support among actors prioritizing ambition and regulatory credibility, while an abrupt schedule may narrow support among actors facing fuel-supply, competitiveness, and infrastructure constraints. Ambition and feasibility should therefore not be treated as alternatives.

Fuel availability, affordability, and scalability, lifecycle certification, bunkering infrastructure, port readiness, and financing capacity will differ across regions and routes. Circular Letter No. 5213 illustrates a market-readiness approach by defining commercially viable fuels through affordability, availability, and scalability and linking those criteria to periodic trajectory review [67] (Annex, reg. 2.3.20 and regs. 31, 35, and 41). These conditions may inform intermediate GFI schedules, review triggers, and targeted support. They should not, however, operate as automatic grounds for weakening the long-term ambition floor, since the framework is intended to influence rather than merely reflect current investment and fuel-supply conditions.

Compliance flexibility should make the transition achievable without making it optional. Three safeguards follow. First, fuel and technology neutrality should be maintained within credible lifecycle GHG accounting [70]. Second, compliance flexibility should help actors move from obligation to capability, through finance, infrastructure, certification support, and technical review. Where demonstrated capability gaps cannot be addressed immediately through support, limited adjustments to implementation timing may be considered, provided that they are time-limited, reviewable, and converge on the common ambition floor rather than repeatedly weakening GFI requirements or the compliance signal. Third, unit-based and certificate-based mechanisms, including banking or the transfer of verified surplus units and book-and-claim-style arrangements, may address early temporal or geographical mismatches between fuel supply and demand, but require robust registries, traceability, additionality, strict limits on any borrowing against future compliance, no double counting, and transparent claims [113].

6.4. Sequencing Core Functions and Adjustable Parameters

The fourth implication concerns maintaining acceptability across procedural stages through adaptive sequencing. As used here, adaptive sequencing distinguishes among three layers: core regulatory functions that should remain protected, regulatory parameters that may be adjusted through specified review procedures, and implementation rules that can evolve with technical and market conditions. This distinction matters because approval or formal adoption does not by itself stabilize a two-level agreement. Level II constraints can evolve as implementation costs become clearer, industries mobilize, fuel markets develop, and political priorities change [114] (pp. 178–183).

The first layer comprises the core functions proposed here: an IMO-centered global framework, a progressively tightening lifecycle-GFI ambition floor, an effective compliance and investment signal, and credible and accessible enabling support subject to transparent and reviewable governance. Protecting these functions does not require every institutional form to remain fixed. Precise payment channels and fund architecture may remain negotiable, provided that the framework continues to deliver credible compliance, support, and accountability functions. The second layer consists of reviewable regulatory parameters, including intermediate GFI values and timelines, remedial-unit prices, payment or contribution formulas, ZNZ reward levels, and revenue-allocation parameters. The third layer comprises implementation rules governing lifecycle factors, fuel certification, reporting and verification, registry operation, access procedures, and coordination with regional or national measures. Adjustments to the second and third layers should be transparent, based on published evidence, and undertaken pursuant to specified review clauses. Reviews may consider verified fuel-supply or infrastructure gaps, material increases in compliance costs, market illiquidity, food-security impacts, persistent under-disbursement of support, or integrity failures. These conditions should trigger assessment rather than automatic relaxation.

This distinction matters both before adoption and during later implementation. Before adoption, clarifications, guidelines, and targeted adjustments can help conditional supporters assess domestic and sectoral implications but should not substitute for agreement on the core functions. The adjournment could be used to clarify lifecycle benchmarks, review criteria, fuel-supply evidence, support arrangements, and incentives for early uptake of compliant fuels and technologies [18]. After adoption and during implementation, specified review clauses should permit bounded adjustment without reopening the core functions. The draft amendments approved for circulation already provide for a review of remedial-unit prices from 2031, periodic determination of ZNZ rewards and revenue allocation, continuous review of food-security impacts, and a five-year review of the chapter [5] (regs. 36.10, 39.3, 40.7, 43.2 and 44.1). These provisions illustrate how adjustment can be built into the framework, although their value will depend on the scope, evidence requirements, and decision rules governing review. Sequencing in this form may support a more durable agreement space by protecting core functions while allowing for a bounded adjustment of parameters that are particularly consequential for conditional supporters.

7. Conclusions

The sequence from approval for circulation at MEPC 83 to adjournment at MEPC/ES.2 suggests that the coalition sufficient at the approval stage was not durable enough to support timely adoption. Using the two-level game framework, this article interprets that sequence through three linked Level I contestations: rule-making authority, responsibility allocation, and transition pathway design. These issues were filtered through different Level II constraints. The relevant constraints cut across non-exclusive actor configurations and included regulatory credibility, sovereignty and cost concerns, trade exposure, climate vulnerability, fuel availability, fleet competitiveness, and legal certainty. This pattern supports the article’s argument that the negotiations cannot be reduced to a simple North–South or ambition-resistance divide. Because the analysis relies on public documents, it identifies indicative acceptance conditions rather than directly observable win-set boundaries. Later-stage records, delegation-level interviews, and comparison with other multilateral regulatory processes could test these interpretations and propositions.

The central policy implication is that a maritime decarbonization regime requires more than technically sound instruments; it requires the resulting package to remain politically supportable across successive stages. A more durable agreement space would likely require an IMO-centered framework with bounded and accountable economic governance; generally uniform core obligations paired with needs-based enabling support and accountable revenue use; an ambition floor combined with feasible compliance pathways; and a clear distinction between core functions and adjustable parameters. These conditions do not eliminate distributive conflicts or guarantee adoption. They instead identify design conditions that may help a global framework remain environmentally meaningful, legally defensible, and politically supportable.

The theoretical implications may extend beyond international shipping, subject to the limits of a single case. Three tentative propositions follow for staged multilateral regulatory processes. First, coalition sufficiency is stage-dependent: approval-stage support may represent only a provisional coalition, because later stages activate different decision rules and make anticipated costs more salient. Second, issue linkage may facilitate provisional coalition formation while also increasing its later vulnerability when distributive, institutional, and transition-related consequences become more visible. Third, durability depends not only on the size of the Level I coalition, but also on whether the package remains defensible across heterogeneous Level II settings as costs, constituencies, and political pressures change. These propositions suggest that two-level game analysis should attend not only to agreement formation, but also to whether an agreement space can be sustained across approval, adoption, acceptance, entry into force, and implementation. In staged multilateral regulation, durability may therefore depend on adjusting politically consequential parameters under transparent review without weakening the regulatory core.

text:
In attesa di capire quale sarà, o quali saranno, i fuel decarbonizzati che consentiranno allo shipping di abbattere drasticamente le proprie emissioni nel lungo termine, e rispettare gli standard internazionali, sempre più armatori stanno puntando sul bioGNL, ovvero il biometano liquefatto, e sugli altri biocombustibili già disponibili grazie a tecnologie sostanzialmente mature.

A conferma di ciò, nei giorni scorsi nel porto di Shanghai è stata completata la più grande operazione al mondo di bunkeraggio di biometanolo effettuata in un’unica soluzione, con la fornitura di 8.016 tonnellate di biometanolo in una singola operazione alla portacontainer CMA CGM Osmium, nave della compagnia francese CMA CGM, terzo liner al mondo per capacità della flotta.

Si tratta – come spiega la stessa società transalpina in una nota pubblicata sul proprio profilo Linkedin – di un volume sufficiente a coprire l’intero viaggio della nave da Shanghai alla costa orientale del Sud America, con una riduzione stimata delle emissioni equivalente a 10.000 tonnellate di CO2.

Realizzata in collaborazione con Shanghai Electric Group e Shanghai International Port (Group), questa operazione – sottolinea CMA CGM – “dimostra il potenziale del biometanolo per applicazioni marittime su larga scala e contribuisce allo sviluppo di soluzioni basate su combustibili a minore intensità di carbonio per il trasporto marittimo”.

Ma l’industria marittima sta guardando con crescente attenzione anche al biometano liquefatto, come evidenzia una recente analisi della fondazione Mærsk Mc-Kinney Møller Center for Zero Carbon Shipping, legata al gruppo danese Maersk, il secondo armatore al mondo (dietro a MSC e davanti proprio a CMA CGM) nel settore container.

Lo studio definisce il biometano “un vettore energetico ormai consolidato, tecnologicamente maturo e compatibile con le infrastrutture esistenti, capace realisticamente di crescere fino a soddisfare la domanda generata dalla regolamentazione”, ovvero dalla bozza del Net-Zero Framework dell’International Maritime Organization (IMO NZF), che la fondazione danese ha utilizzato come riferimento, pur trattandosi di uno schema normativo che non è ancora stato adottato in via definitiva.

Nello specifico, il Mærsk Mc-Kinney Møller Center for Zero Carbon Shipping stima che l’offerta globale di biometano potrebbe raggiungere circa 21 bcm (billion cubic meters) nel 2030 in uno scenario “base” e 52 bcm in uno scenario “max”, sostenuto dalle politiche pubbliche. Entrambi i valori rimangono molto inferiori al potenziale tecnico globale indicato dall’International Energy Agency (IEA), suggerendo che i principali vincoli sono rappresentati dalle infrastrutture, dalla certificazione, dalla regolamentazione e dall’accesso alle filiere del gas e del GNL, piuttosto che dalla disponibilità delle biomasse utilizzabili come materia prima.

In questo scenario, il dossier evidenzia il ruolo cruciale svolto dai requisiti di certificazione: “Senza un sistema di mass balance riconosciuto a livello globale, lo shipping dovrebbe probabilmente fare affidamento su filiere di approvvigionamento del biometano fisicamente separate, difficili e costose da sviluppare su larga scala. Attualmente, tuttavia, la contabilizzazione tramite mass balance rimane uno degli ostacoli principali e richiederebbe maggiore chiarezza normativa”.

Ma se questo e altri fattori abilitanti venissero effettivamente implementati, secondo il centro studi danese la quantità di energia disponibile da questo vettore, sulla base di ipotesi plausibili, potrebbe essere considerevole e potrebbe quindi contribuire alla riduzione delle emissioni dell’industria marittima.

Va tuttavia rilevato che lo shipping sarà probabilmente in competizione con altri settori per le stesse molecole di biometano: una maggiore disponibilità a pagare da parte di altri comparti potrebbe quindi ridurre l’accesso del trasporto marittimo a questa soluzione di decarbonizzazione.

In definitiva, la disponibilità di materie prime in prossimità della rete del gas non rappresenta il principale fattore limitante prima del 2030. La questione fondamentale – conclude lo studio – è invece se lo shipping potrà accedere a questo più ampio sistema basato sul gas attraverso un meccanismo certificato di mass balancing.
